When higher yields hurt the price but help later cash: chart a bond’s investment horizon

Follow sale value, coupons and reinvestment growth across time, reconcile the offsetting effects and test cash dates against constant yield scenarios in four charts.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare a bond’s sale value with growth on its received cash flows

Interactive planning lab

Original purchase price before the yield change$100,000
Macaulay duration at purchase · model years8.1
Changed-yield wealth minus unchanged-yield wealth at selected date-$62.57

Original deterministic annual-coupon bond illustration, with no observed bond data or quoted security. Purchase occurs immediately after a coupon boundary. The selected yield changes once immediately after purchase and then stays constant; that same effective annual rate prices every remaining payment and reinvests all received coupons and maturity principal. All payments occur in full on schedule; no default, call, fees, spread, tax, inflation, FX, curve twists or later rate changes. Wealth before maturity includes an assumed immediate sale at model value; after maturity it includes reinvested principal instead. No amount is counted twice. Reinvested cash must remain invested until the comparison date; using coupons for spending changes the result. Duration is a local sensitivity measure, not a guaranteed risk-free horizon.

The central idea

A bond’s immediate price reaction and the cash available years later answer different questions. The comparison date and the reinvestment assumptions determine how the two effects combine.

01

Begin with the same bond and two different yield paths

The example buys a hypothetical bond with CAD 100,000 face value, a fixed 5% annual coupon and ten years to maturity. Its purchase yield is 5% effective annually, so the purchase price is CAD 100,000. The purchase occurs immediately after a coupon boundary, with no accrued interest or dealing cost.

Immediately afterward, the selected scenario changes the yield to 7%. It then keeps that yield constant for pricing every remaining payment and reinvesting every receipt. The comparison leaves the yield at 5%. Both own the same contractual cash flows and begin with the same purchase outlay.

The SEC’s fixed-income bulletin explains the inverse relationship between fixed-rate bond prices and market yields. This article adds an explicit cash ledger so that the immediate price effect can be read beside the later reinvestment effect.

02

The first plotted value comes after the yield change

The line chart starts at time zero immediately after the hypothetical rate change. In the changed-yield scenario, the remaining payments are discounted at 7%, so the bond’s value is below the original CAD 100,000 purchase price. The 5% comparison begins at the original price.

A lower initial point is not a new deposit or a withdrawal. It is a change in the model sale value. The two scenarios still receive the same CAD 5,000 coupon at the end of each year and the same CAD 100,000 face amount at maturity.

Each subsequent point falls immediately after that year’s payment. Before maturity, plotted wealth combines the assumed sale value of unpaid bond cash flows with cash already received and reinvested. At and after maturity, there is no outstanding bond: the model replaces it with received principal, which also earns the selected reinvestment rate.

03

An early cash date can be dominated by the price effect

At the end of year one, the 7% scenario has CAD 86,969.54 of remaining bond sale value and the just-paid CAD 5,000 coupon. The coupon has had no time to earn additional interest. Together they give CAD 91,969.54.

The unchanged-yield comparison has CAD 100,000 of bond value plus the same CAD 5,000 coupon, totaling CAD 105,000. The changed-yield result is CAD 13,030.46 lower. It is also CAD 8,030.46 below the original purchase outlay. Those are different comparisons and should be labelled separately.

The chart assumes that the remaining bond can be sold immediately at its calculated value. A real household cash goal also needs a buyer, settlement time and usable proceeds. The model includes no bid–ask spread, liquidity restriction or credit deterioration, so it cannot establish the actual amount available from a sale.

04

Read the year-eight offset in its original units

At the default eight-year horizon, the changed-yield sale value is CAD 96,383.96. Eight coupons originally contributed CAD 40,000 of cash. Reinvesting those coupons at 7% grows their combined value to CAD 51,299.01, including CAD 11,299.01 of growth. Total modeled wealth is CAD 147,682.98.

The 5% comparison has CAD 100,000 of sale value and CAD 47,745.54 of accumulated coupon cash, for CAD 147,745.54. The changed-yield result is only about CAD 62.57 lower at this date, despite its much larger early price disadvantage.

The waterfall explains the reconciliation: sale value is CAD 3,616.04 lower, while growth on received cash is CAD 3,553.47 higher. The original coupon amounts cancel because the contracts are identical. Adding a separate coupon difference would count a change that never occurred.

05

Duration explains a local balance, rather than a guaranteed finish

Macaulay duration is the present-value-weighted average payment time. For this example, calculate the present value of each annual cash flow at the original 5% yield, multiply each by its payment year, add those weighted amounts and divide by the purchase price. The result is approximately 8.10782 model years.

The CFA Institute’s public interest-rate-risk overview connects investment horizon with price and coupon-reinvestment effects. In this constant-yield model, choosing a horizon equal to the original duration makes the first-order effect of a small immediate yield change zero.

That is a local mathematical result. The selected eight-year horizon is close to, rather than exactly equal to, 8.10782 years. A two-percentage-point change is also a finite change. Do not expect identical wealth for every large rate movement, or treat an originally matched duration as a permanent hedge against later changes in the yield curve.

06

Use a cash-flow identity to check the result

Let CFt be the coupon plus any principal due at year t, H the comparison date and y the constant post-purchase annual yield as a fraction. Each received payment grows forward to H; each unpaid payment is discounted back to H. The combined value is W(y,H) = Σ CFt(1+y)H−t.

The same expression equals P(y) × (1+y)H, where P(y) is the value at time zero of all remaining payments discounted at y. This identity checks the complete cash ledger; it does not mean the investor originally paid the changed-yield price P(y). The actual purchase price remains the value calculated using the original yield.

For a positive horizon, annualized wealth return is (horizon wealth ÷ actual purchase price)1/H − 1. The unchanged 5% case produces 5% under these reinvestment assumptions. The default changed-yield eight-year case produces about 4.99444%. A coupon percentage alone would not supply either complete result.

07

Maturity removes the outstanding bond, but not every reinvestment question

At year ten, both cases have received the same CAD 100,000 principal and CAD 50,000 of original coupons. The 7% case has accumulated CAD 19,082.24 of coupon-reinvestment growth; the 5% case has CAD 12,889.46. Their wealth totals are CAD 169,082.24 and CAD 162,889.46, a difference of CAD 6,192.78.

There is no remaining sale-price difference at this point because the assumed principal payment has occurred in both cases. For later dates, the model reinvests that principal too. It does not leave principal inside an already matured bond or add it a second time to an outstanding bond value.

If the household instead spends each coupon, those amounts are unavailable to compound toward this cash goal. If principal is needed immediately at maturity, no later principal-reinvestment income belongs in that goal. Use the actual intended treatment of receipts when interpreting the chart.

08

Use the matrix to expose the date assumption

The matrix changes the cash date and the constant post-purchase yield. Each cell subtracts the unchanged-yield wealth at that same date. A negative value describes a disadvantage against that comparison, while a positive value describes an advantage. Neither is a probability or a statement that the household’s required payment is funded.

This model deliberately excludes default, calls, changing credit spreads, taxes, fees, inflation, foreign currency and later rate changes. Its annual coupons and flat discount rate are teaching conventions. Actual securities may have different payment schedules and contractual options.

For a real goal, begin with its required cash date, verify the security’s payment schedule and consider what happens if a sale is required earlier. Then document the treatment of each coupon and maturity receipt. The four charts help reveal those assumptions before an attractive yield is treated as a complete financial plan.
